description: We are CookingCoders, a team of creative problem-solvers passionate about coding, AI, engineering, and innovation. Just like cooking, we believe the best solutions come from combining the right ingredients: teamwork, creativity, and technology. Our goal is to tackle real-world challenges, develop innovative projects, and turn ideas into reality. We're excited to collaborate, learn new skills, and cook up something amazing at the NASA Space Apps Challenge!
summary:
Field Shift is an interactive farming simulator that uses historical NASA Earth data to help users explore how weather and farming decisions affect soil water availability.

Our project uses NASA POWER weather data to simulate rainfall, irrigation, evapotranspiration, and soil-water storage over time. Users can customize their farm's location, crop, soil type, growing season, irrigation, and ground cover, then watch how these decisions affect the simulated farm.

Field Shift also provides a model-based farm score, identifies potential problems such as water shortages or excessive irrigation, and allows users to compare different management choices.

We developed Field Shift to make complex NASA climate data easier to understand and useful for exploring agricultural decisions. Although our current prototype focuses on soil-water management rather than complete crop-rotation modeling, it demonstrates how NASA data can support more informed and sustainable farming decisions.
details:
What is Field Shift?

Field Shift is an interactive farming simulation platform that uses historical NASA Earth data to help users explore how weather and agricultural decisions affect soil-water availability.

Our goal is to make NASA's environmental data easier to understand and turn complex scientific calculations into an interactive experience.

How It Works

Field Shift uses daily weather data from NASA's Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) project, including precipitation, temperature, humidity, solar radiation, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure.

Users can customize seven settings:

  • Farm location
  • Historical weather year
  • Crop type
  • Soil type
  • Growing season
  • Irrigation amount
  • Ground cover

The simulator processes these inputs using a daily soil-water balance model. It calculates how water enters the soil through rainfall and irrigation, how water is lost through evapotranspiration, and how excess water drains below the modeled soil layer.

Users can watch these conditions change through an animated farm visualization.

Field Shift also produces a provisional farm score out of 100, identifies the biggest modeled problem, and tests alternative irrigation and ground-cover scenarios. Users can prioritize reducing crop-water shortages, saving irrigation water, or balancing both.

Technology Used

We developed Field Shift using JavaScript, React, HTML, CSS, and Vite for the interactive website.

Python was used to retrieve, process, and validate NASA POWER weather data. The simulation uses FAO-56 evapotranspiration methods and documented soil-water assumptions.

GitHub was used to manage our source code, and Vercel hosts the website.

AI-assisted development tools helped us implement, debug, test, and refine the application.

Creativity and Innovation

Instead of presenting NASA data through static graphs, we created an interactive visual simulation that lets users experiment with different farm settings and watch their consequences over time.

The scoring system evaluates modeled crop-water supply, irrigation efficiency, and precipitation exposure. It also tests alternatives using the same historical weather so users can compare outcomes fairly.

Impact and Limitations

Field Shift aims to make NASA Earth data more accessible to students, researchers, and people interested in sustainable agriculture.

Our prototype focuses on water management, an important part of agricultural planning. Although the original challenge emphasizes crop rotations, our current simulator does not predict complete multi-year rotation outcomes.

The model uses representative Washington locations and generic soil parameters rather than measurements from individual farms. Its scores are educational estimates, not validated agricultural recommendations.

We hope Field Shift demonstrates how NASA data can support future agricultural decision-making tools while making scientific uncertainty clear.
